title: A Tribe Steals Its Gods and Home
overview: The tribe of Dan, still without land of its own, steals a private shrine and its priest, then wipes out a peaceful town in the far north and makes it their home.

parts.label: Dan looks for a home (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: The tribe of Dan still had no settled land of its own, so they sent five scouts north to find somewhere to live. At Micah's private shrine they asked his hired priest whether they would succeed, and he gave them the warm answer they hoped for.

parts.label: An easy target (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: Laish was rich, peaceful and far from any allies, and the story keeps stressing how unsuspecting its people were. The scouts said God had handed it to them, though the story never says God told them to take it.

parts.label: Robbing Micah's shrine (vv. 11-21)
parts.note: While 600 armed men blocked the gate, the scouts took Micah's silver idol, his household gods (small figurines) and his ephod, a priestly garment used to ask God questions. Offered a whole tribe instead of one household, the priest gladly went along.

parts.label: Micah's helpless protest (vv. 22-26)
parts.note: Micah chased them, complaining that they had taken the gods he made and left him nothing. The Danites simply threatened to kill him and his family, so he went home, a picture of a time when the strong took what they wanted.

parts.label: Laish destroyed, idol set up (vv. 27-31)
parts.note: They killed the people of Laish, burned the town and rebuilt it as Dan, which became Israel's northern edge, and set up the stolen idol there while the house of God stood at Shiloh. The priest is named as Jonathan, descended from Moses through Gershom, and his family served this shrine until the 'captivity of the land,' which scholars usually link to the Assyrian conquest of the north in the 700s BC, though they are not certain.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the taking of Laish should be seen as part of God's earlier promise of the land or as a lawless land grab the narrator presents with clear disapproval.
think: How do you tell the difference between advice you can trust and advice that simply tells you what you already hoped to hear?
